title: Adverbial clauses of time
subtitle: as / when / while; until; no sooner ... than
summary: Choose between as, when and while, use before and until precisely, and build sentences with hardly, no sooner and scarcely.

lesson.heading: as, when and while = 'during the time that'
lesson.text: All three can introduce something that happens at the time when something else takes place.

examples.text: **As / When / While** Miguel was eating, the doorbell rang.
I packed all the books away **while / as** Lana made a note of their titles on her laptop.

lesson.heading: when only
lesson.text: We use **when** (not as or while) for an event that takes place at the same time as some longer event, and for the circumstances in which the event in the main clause happens. We also use when to mean 'every time', and we prefer it for past periods of our lives.

examples.text: They were playing in the garden **when** they heard a scream.
**When** they are fully grown these snakes can be over two metres long.
I still feel tired **when** I wake up in the morning.
His mother called him Robbie **when** he was a baby.

lesson.heading: when for one thing straight after another
lesson.text: We prefer **when** if one event happens immediately after another, particularly if one causes the other.

examples.text: You'll see my house on the right **when** you cross the bridge.
**When** the lights went out, I lit some candles.

lesson.note: In the first sentence, as or while would suggest 'during the time that', and the continuous would then be more likely (as / while you are crossing ...). In the second, as or while would be very unlikely, because lights usually go out instantaneously.

lesson.heading: as for parallel change, while for two long actions

left.label: as - as one thing changes, another changes
examples: **As** the cheese matures, its flavour improves.
rather than When the cheese matures ...
The humidity started to increase **as** the day wore on.

right.label: while or as - two longer actions at the same time
examples: I went shopping **while** Liam cleaned the house.
The snow was getting deeper and deeper **while / as** we waited for the train.

lesson.note: 'While the cheese is maturing ...' is also possible, particularly with a continuous tense. While is more common than as in informal speech.

lesson.heading: Avoiding the 'because' reading of as
lesson.text: We use **while** or **when** rather than as where 'as' could be understood to mean 'because'.

examples.text: **While** you were playing golf, I went to the cinema.
examples.note: As you were playing golf ... could mean 'Because ...'

examples.text: She stayed at home watching television **while / when** her brother was at school.

lesson.heading: before, after and until
lesson.text: **Before** and **after** say that an event happened earlier or later than another. We can often use either **until** or **before** when a situation continues up to a time given in the adverbial clause. But we use until for an action that continues to a particular time and then stops, and when the adverbial clause describes the result of the action in the main clause.

examples.text: I put on my coat **before** I went out. / The message arrived **after** I'd left.
I had to wait six weeks **until / before** the parcel arrived.
They sat on the beach **until** the sun sank below the horizon, and then they went home.
He cleaned his shoes **until** they shone.
examples.note: shining is the result of cleaning

lesson.heading: hardly, no sooner, scarcely
lesson.text: To say that one event happened immediately after another we can use **hardly**, **no sooner** and **scarcely**. After hardly and scarcely the second clause begins with **when** or **before**; after no sooner it begins with **than** or **when**.

examples.text: The concert had **hardly** begun **before** all the lights went out.
I had **no sooner** lit the barbecue **than / when** it started to rain.
I had **scarcely** driven to the end of the street **when** the engine cut out.

lesson.note: We usually use a past perfect in the clause with hardly, no sooner or scarcely, and a past simple in the other.

lesson.text: *no sooner ... than* is the pair to remember - hardly and scarcely take *when* or *before* instead.

exercises.prompt: ___ we were younger our parents had to pay for our music lessons.
exercises.explanation: We prefer when for a past period of our lives.

exercises.prompt: The humidity started to increase ___ the day wore on.
exercises.explanation: As shows that one thing changed while another changed alongside it.

exercises.prompt: Where did you live ___ you got married?
exercises.explanation: Getting married is a single point in time, not a period, so when is needed.

exercises.prompt: She stayed at home watching television ___ her brother was at school.
exercises.explanation: As is avoided here because it could be read as 'because'.

exercises.statement: I was in the shower as the phone rang.
exercises.explanation: I was in the shower when the phone rang. When introduces a short event happening during a longer one.

exercises.statement: As I'm older I'd love to be a dancer.
exercises.explanation: When I'm older I'd love to be a dancer. This is the circumstance in which the main clause will apply, so when is needed.

exercises.prompt: The disk drive makes a buzzing sound ___ I switch my PlayStation on.
exercises.explanation: Switching on is instantaneous and causes the sound, so when is right; while and as would suggest 'during the time that'.

exercises.prompt: He continued to work at London University ___ he retired in 2007.
exercises.explanation: The action continued up to that point and then stopped, so only until works.

exercises.prompt: He married Martha ___ he moved to England in 1960.
exercises.explanation: One event simply happened earlier than the other, so before.

exercises.prompt: Complete each gap with before or until. Which gaps allow both?
categories: Both before and until are possible

items.text: He applied for research positions ___ he was appointed to a post at London University.
It wasn't long ___ he was appointed Professor of Chemistry.
He would work in his lab for days at a time ___ he had completed an experiment.
___ he came to England he worked in his father's grocery shop.
He was almost unknown outside his field ___ he was awarded the Nobel Prize.

exercises.prompt: Say that the rain started the moment the barbecue was lit.
exercises.answer: I had no sooner lit the barbecue than it started to rain.
exercises.explanation: No sooner is followed by than (or when), with a past perfect in the first clause and a past simple in the second.

exercises.prompt: Match each first clause to the event that followed immediately.

pairs.left: The paint on the sitting room wall had scarcely dried
pairs.right: before my daughter put her dirty hands all over it.

pairs.left: Martin had no sooner recovered from a broken ankle
He had hardly put down the phone

pairs.right: before members of the audience started to criticise her.

pairs.left: I had scarcely driven to the end of the street
